lesson.title: Two-step sign-in and passkeys
lesson.subtitle: A stolen password is no longer enough

video.title: Two-step sign-in and passkeys
video.format_note: Animated explainer, 16:9, flat Darsi colours on paper-grey backgrounds; narration in the lesson language, captions as separate files.
cast: Mr Joseph Mwangi — computer studies teacher (main character)
Narrator — the Darsi voice (warm, peer to peer)

scenes.visual: Okafor at his kitchen table at night. His phone lights up: “Someone is trying to sign in.” A shadowy figure outside a door holds a key labelled “password”, but a second lock on the door stays shut.
scenes.animation: Phone glows; the figure rattles the second lock.
scenes.narration: Last night my phone said, “Someone is trying to sign in to your email.” They had my password. But they still couldn’t get in. Why not?

scenes.visual: Title card with the Darsi mark and the cyber track chip.
scenes.animation: Mark pops in; title slides up.
scenes.narration: Today: two-step sign-in, passkeys, and why a stolen password alone is no longer enough.

scenes.visual: Three proof cards: a key (know), a phone (have), a fingerprint (are). A thief holds only the key card and stands outside a door with two locks.
scenes.animation: Cards deal in one by one; the thief’s key opens one lock, the second stays shut.
scenes.narration: Two-step sign-in asks for two kinds of proof. Something you know, like your password. Something you have, like your phone. Or something you are, like your fingerprint. A thief with your password still doesn’t have your phone, so they’re stuck.

scenes.visual: A ladder of three steps: a text bubble with a code, an app with a code and a small timer, and a fingerprint with a key. Each step is higher and greener than the one before.
scenes.animation: Steps rise one at a time; the app timer ticks round.
scenes.narration: Not all second steps are equal. A code by text message is better than nothing, but a criminal can trick your phone company into moving your number to their SIM. An authenticator app makes a new code every thirty seconds, right on your phone. Strongest of all are passkeys.

scenes.visual: Clean card: a thumb on a phone’s fingerprint reader; a key shape travels to a website that has a green check. A fake website next to it gets nothing.
scenes.animation: The key glides to the real site; the fake site stays grey.
scenes.narration: A passkey lets you sign in with your phone’s fingerprint, face or screen lock. There’s no password to type, and nothing a scammer can copy. And a passkey only works on the real website, so a fake page gets nothing. Google, Microsoft, Apple and WhatsApp accounts already offer them.

scenes.visual: Okafor holds up his phone showing a prompt: “Are you trying to sign in?” with Yes and No. Three answer cards drop in.
scenes.animation: Cards drop in with a small bounce.
scenes.narration: Quick check. My phone asks, “Are you trying to sign in?” But I’m not signing in to anything. What do I do?

scenes.visual: The “deny” card gets the check badge. Okafor taps No, then types a new password. In the corner, prompts keep stacking up; each one gets a calm No.
scenes.animation: Check badge pops; prompts stack and are crossed out.
scenes.narration: Deny it, then change your password, because someone out there has it. Never approve a prompt you didn’t start, however many times it asks. Some attackers send prompt after prompt, hoping you’ll tap yes just to make it stop.

scenes.visual: Three doors in a row: an envelope door (email) with a master key hanging on it, a chat door with a six-digit keypad, and a door with a banknote and a school sign.
scenes.animation: Doors lock one after another, left to right.
scenes.narration: Where do you start? With your email, because it can reset every other account. Then WhatsApp: turn on two-step verification, and choose a six-digit PIN. Then your mobile money, your school account and anything with pupils’ data.

scenes.visual: A phone falls out of a bag. A sheet of paper with a list of codes sits in a drawer at home; a spare key hangs beside it.
scenes.animation: Drawer slides open; the spare key glints.
scenes.narration: What if your phone is lost? When you turn on two-step sign-in, you’re given backup codes. Write them down on paper, and keep them at home, not in your phone. They’re your spare key.

scenes.visual: Two warning cards. One: a caller saying “I’m from the bank, read me the code.” Two: a phone status bar showing “No service”, with a phone company building beside it.
scenes.animation: Warning triangles pulse on each card.
scenes.narration: Two warning signs to know. Anyone who asks for your code is a scammer, even if they say they’re the bank, or a friend. And if your phone suddenly shows “No service” for no reason, call your phone company at once: someone may be moving your number.

scenes.visual: Joseph points at three options on a board: a text bubble, an app, a fingerprint. Three answer cards bounce in.
scenes.animation: Cards bounce in one by one.
scenes.narration: Your turn. A colleague can choose a text message code, an authenticator app or a passkey. Which is strongest?

scenes.visual: The passkey card gets the check badge. Four summary cards line up.
scenes.animation: Cards line up left to right, 250 ms apart.
scenes.on_screen_text: Two proofs · Deny · Email first · Backup codes
scenes.narration: A passkey: it can’t be phished, and there’s no code to steal. Remember: two kinds of proof, deny prompts you didn’t start, start with your email, and keep your backup codes on paper.

scenes.visual: Joseph’s classroom. A pupil in a paper “thief” mask holds a card marked “password”; classmates hold up cards for a second lock.
scenes.animation: Second-lock cards pop up around the room.
scenes.narration: Try it in class tomorrow: play “Two locks”. One pupil plays a thief who knows the password, and the class decides which second step stops the thief, and why.

checkpoints.prompt: A sign-in prompt pops up on your phone, but you aren’t signing in. What do you do?

options.text: Deny it, then change your password
Ignore it and wait for it to go away

checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct: someone has your password. Denying shuts the door, and a new password takes their key away.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite: approving lets the thief in, and ignoring lets them keep trying. Deny it and change your password.

checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct: a passkey can’t be phished, and it can’t be moved to another SIM.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite: codes can be tricked out of you, and text messages can be moved to another SIM. A passkey only works on the real site.
